title: Design a Distributed Cache (like Redis/Memcached) — consistent hashing, cache eviction (LRU/LFU), cache invalidation strategies, write-through vs write-behind, cache stampede prevention.

s1_definition.profdef: A distributed cache is an in-memory key-value store spread across many nodes that serves hot data at microsecond latency to reduce load on slower backing databases. Its core design concerns are distributing keys across nodes with consistent hashing to minimize movement when nodes change, evicting data under memory pressure with policies like least-recently-used or least-frequently-used, invalidating stale entries, choosing a write policy such as write-through or write-behind, and preventing cache stampedes when a hot key expires.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps a small, fast desk of frequently needed records right at the front counter, instead of walking to the big vault archive for every request. When a teller needs Rajesh's balance, they glance at the front desk first. The front desk has limited space, so old records are removed to make room. Multiple front desks across branches must agree on who holds which record, and when a balance changes, the front-desk copy must be refreshed or discarded so nobody reads a stale number. That front-desk system, scaled and automated, is a distributed cache.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spread keys across nodes with consistent hashing, evict with LRU or LFU, keep entries fresh with invalidation, pick a write policy, and guard hot keys against stampedes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A distributed cache is an in-memory key-value store spread across many nodes that serves hot data at microsecond latency to reduce load on slower backing databases. Its core design concerns are distributing keys across nodes with consistent hashing to minimize movement when nodes change, evicting data under memory pressure with policies like least-recently-used or least-frequently-used, invalidating stale entries, choosing a write policy such as write-through or write-behind, and preventing cache stampedes when a hot key expires.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India keeps a small, fast desk of frequently needed records right at the front counter, instead of walking to the big vault archive for every request. When a teller needs Rajesh's balance, they glance at the front desk first. The front desk has limited space, so old records are removed to make room. Multiple front desks across branches must agree on who holds which record, and when a balance changes, the front-desk copy must be refreshed or discarded so nobody reads a stale number. That front-desk system, scaled and automated, is a distributed cache.

**One line to remember:** Spread keys across nodes with consistent hashing, evict with LRU or LFU, keep entries fresh with invalidation, pick a write policy, and guard hot keys against stampedes.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India shows Rajesh's balance on every app screen, and reading it from the main database millions of times a day overloads the database. The real problem is serving hot reads fast without hammering the database. This is exactly what a cache does, and consistent hashing spreads those cached balances across many cache nodes.

Problem 2 — when Rajesh's balance changes after a transfer, the cached copy must not be allowed to show the old value even for a moment, because a wrong balance in banking is unacceptable. This is exactly how write-through and event-based invalidation keep the cache correct.

Problem 3 — a hugely popular key, like the bank's current fixed deposit rate, expires at midnight, and suddenly a million app opens all miss the cache and slam the database. This is exactly the cache stampede, solved with a single-flight lock.

We build a runnable distributed cache core: a `ConsistentHashRing` for node placement, an `LruCache` per node with eviction, a `CacheService` doing write-through and event invalidation, and a `StampedeGuard` single-flight. The demo places balance keys across nodes, serves cached reads, invalidates on a transfer, and shows a stampede on a hot key handled by one rebuild while others wait.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three keys in the database, a cache with three nodes and a capacity of two entries each, and a sequence of reads, a write, and a stampede on the fixed deposit rate key.

Step 1: The consistent hash ring maps each key to a node. Rajesh's balance key lands on one node, the rate key on another, decided by where their hashes fall on the ring.

Step 2: The first read of Rajesh's balance misses the cache, so it loads from the slow database and populates the cache. The second read hits the cache and returns instantly without touching the database.

Step 3: A transfer calls write-through. The new balance of nine hundred fifty thousand is saved to the database first, then written into the cache, so the very next read returns the fresh value and never a stale one.

Step 4: The rate key is invalidated, then three threads read it at once. The stampede guard lets only one thread acquire the lock and rebuild from the database; the other two wait and then read the value the first thread just cached, so the database is hit once instead of three times.

```
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] balance:SAV2001 -> cache-B
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] read1 1000000
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] read2 1000000
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] write-through balance:SAV2001=950000
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] after write 950000
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] invalidated fd:rate
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] single rebuild of fd:rate
2026-10-31 23:10:00 [INFO] served by waiter fd:rate
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  key "balance:SAV2001"
    │ ConsistentHashRing.nodeFor → cache-B
    ▼
  read(key)
    │
    ├─ cache HIT → return (µs)       ├─ cache MISS
    │                                │  db.load (ms, slow)
    │                                │  cache.put
    ▼                                ▼
  value                           value + cached

  writeThrough(balance, 950000)
    │ db.save FIRST (durable)
    │ cache.put (fresh)
    ▼
  next read = 950000 (never stale)

  invalidate(fd:rate) → 3 concurrent reads (STAMPEDE)
    │
    ├─ T1 gets lock → db.load → cache.put
    ├─ T2 waits → reads cached value
    └─ T3 waits → reads cached value
    ▼
  DB hit ONCE, not 3×
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A distributed cache is an in-memory key-value store spread across many nodes that serves hot data at microsecond latency and shields a slower database from the flood of reads. The first design concern is how to distribute keys across nodes, and I use consistent hashing: both nodes and keys sit on a ring, and a key lives on the first node clockwise from its hash. The value of this is that adding or removing a node only moves a small fraction of keys rather than remapping everything, and virtual nodes keep the distribution even.

The second concern is eviction, because cache memory is finite. Least-recently-used drops the entry untouched longest and suits temporal locality, while least-frequently-used drops the rarely accessed entry and suits workloads with permanently hot keys. The third concern is invalidation and the write policy. For anything resembling a bank balance I use write-through, writing to the database first for durability and then updating the cache, combined with event-based invalidation, so the cache is never allowed to show a stale balance. I avoid write-behind for money because it can lose recent writes if a node crashes before flushing, even though it is faster.

In the National Bank of India context, the cache served Rajesh's balance on every app screen so the database was not read millions of times a day, and write-through plus invalidation guaranteed that the instant his balance changed after a transfer, the next read returned the fresh number rather than an old one. That correctness guarantee is non-negotiable in banking.

The subtle problem I always raise is the cache stampede, or thundering herd. When a very popular key like the current fixed deposit rate expires, thousands of requests can miss the cache simultaneously and all slam the database at once. I prevent this with a single-flight lock so only one request rebuilds the value while the others wait and then read the freshly cached result, and I complement it with staggered or probabilistic early expiration so hot keys are refreshed just before they fully expire. Designing for that stampede is the difference between a cache that protects the database and one that accidentally amplifies load at the worst possible moment.
